chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: Irving Mills's composer credits on Ellington music
summary: Barnet and Willard doubt that Irving Mills wrote any of the music he took credit for, though Barnet grants Mills helped shape Ellington's career.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, Irving Mills claims that he took all his raw material and whipped it into shape, and that all of these guys had great ideas and they were just brilliant, but they didn't come up with good names, they didn't write to three minutes, and they didn't know how to make things
commercial. So he would take all this raw material and whip it into shape and for that he got his composer's credit. That's what he told me.
Well, that may be so, but --
I don't know. Do you know what he did?

I knew Irving very well. I always had a very nice relationship with him, but I just don't think that -- I know a story, but I don't know the truth of it, and I wouldn't want to say it on account of that, but I do know that Duke was raised to the top category of ASCAP and Irving's name was on all of the songs and he didn't raise him. So who knows? And you and I know very well, that he may have said, 'Well, we'll call that the 'Dirty River Blues',' and maybe they brought it in and it was the 'Clean River Blues.' This isn't really a terrible lot of talent, to be able to do that.
No. I'm really curious though, whether Duke Ellington learned something valuable from Irving Mills.
Oh, he says he did. He says he did, in his book, you know, 'Music is My Mistress.'
Oh, I have no doubt that Irving Mills contributed a lot into the formation of the giant that was Duke Ellington. But as far as writing any of the music, I'm
I tend to be, too, and I --

I think he was along for the -- that was a common practice. Look, I had it happen to me, Pat. I had guys come in and say, 'You're looking at the guy here --,' a guy came in, we were playing the Lincoln Hotel, and we used to rehearse at night, you know, at 2:00 o'clock in the morning, and we were having a rehearsal, and this guy came in and he said --
